title: Minimax rate of sequential binary calibration
formal:
Determine the minimax expected ordinary calibration error
\[
C(T)=\inf_{P,A}\ \sup_B\ \mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{p\in P}\left|\sum_{\substack{1\le t\le T\\p_t=p}}(y_t-p)\right|\right]
\]
up to absolute multiplicative constants as the integer horizon \(T\) tends to infinity. The finite prediction set \(P\subseteq[0,1]\), forecaster \(A\) and adaptive adversary \(B\) use the simultaneous-move game below. The requested rate includes every logarithmic factor.
definitions:
Fix an integer \(T\ge1\). Before play the forecaster selects a nonempty finite set \(P\subseteq[0,1]\). It may depend on \(T\), and there is no bound on its cardinality or restriction to rational values. Both players know \(T\) and \(P\). At each round \(t\), the forecaster draws \(p_t\in P\) and the adversary draws \(y_t\in\{0,1\}\) simultaneously, after which both values are revealed. Each player's choice may depend on the entire common history \((p_1,y_1),\ldots,(p_{t-1},y_{t-1})\). Neither observes the other player's current draw. Strategies are arbitrary assignments of probability distributions to the finitely many histories of this game; private randomization is independent between the players. There is no computation, memory or bit-precision restriction.

For each fixed \(P,A\), the supremum ranges over all these adaptive adversary strategies, including strategies selected with knowledge of \(A\). The infimum ranges over all finite \(P\) and all forecaster strategies for that set. The players may choose different strategies at different horizons; no one horizon-independent algorithm is required. This is a mathematical minimax value, not the runtime for solving a finite game.

For a realized play, all rounds with exactly the same numerical prediction \(p\) form one group. That group's contribution is the absolute difference between its number of one outcomes and its size times \(p\). An unused prediction contributes zero. Sum these absolute errors before taking expectation over both players' randomization. Thus the loss is the unnormalized \(\ell_1\) calibration error, between zero and \(T\); it is not an average per round, a squared error, or the absolute value of an expected signed error. There are no contexts or additional subgroup requirements. The supremum permits dependence on past forecasts; an adversary restricted to a fixed outcome sequence is a narrower model.

An answer must give an explicit positive function \(f:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{>0}\) and constants \(0<c\le C_0<\infty\), \(T_0\ge1\), such that \(c f(T)\le C(T)\le C_0 f(T)\) for every \(T\ge T_0\). The expression for \(f\) must characterize growth independently of the optimization defining \(C\). There is no efficiency requirement for evaluating that expression, but merely restating the same game value as a supremum, infimum or finite-game solving procedure is not the requested asymptotic characterization.

context_blocks.text: Calibration compares announced probabilities with empirical frequencies separately at each prediction value. The minimax question asks for the unavoidable accumulated mismatch in an adversarial sequence.

The checked primary bounds are \(O(T^{2/3-\delta})\) for some fixed \(\delta>0\), and \(\Omega(T^{0.54389})\). Even an oblivious adversary supplies the latter obstruction, whereas the upper guarantee tolerates adaptive outcomes.

Later improvements for squared calibration use a different loss, and the 2026 multicalibration lower bound explicitly distinguishes its group constraints from marginal calibration. Neither closes this gap.

why: A fundamental quantitative problem in sequential prediction, with consequences for calibrated learning and decision making.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of such an explicit matching rate. The upper bound must work against every allowed adaptive adversary, and the lower bound must cover every finite prediction set and every forecaster. Matching only the power of \(T\) while leaving an unbounded logarithmic gap is insufficient. A bound for squared calibration, multicalibration, or only a fixed prediction grid does not by itself establish this ordinary calibration rate.

progress.text: Theorems 1.3 and 1.4 break the old two-thirds upper exponent and give the \(0.54389\) lower exponent.
The ALT paper proves a soft-\(O(T^{1/3})\) guarantee for its squared calibration measure, not the displayed ordinary absolute-error loss.
The multicalibration revision explicitly contrasts its lower bounds with the smaller known marginal-calibration upper bound.

sentences: A forecaster announces a probability while an adversary simultaneously chooses a binary outcome.
Both players see past forecasts and outcomes, but neither sees the other current choice.
Calibration error adds the absolute frequency mismatch at each exact prediction value.
The target is the smallest worst-case expected error as a function of the horizon, including logarithmic factors.
Known bounds improve on the old two-thirds exponent but leave a gap for this ordinary calibration measure.
